paragraphs.source_en: It was the assignation of the locus of all radical spiritual claims, whether Magnificence 155 made by Savafid Shi’is or by Ottoman Sunnis, to their proper place—the body of Suleiman I. Unlike in Christian Europe—where church councils determined orthodoxy, condemned nonconforming beliefs as heresies, and persecuted the dissenters as heretics—in the Ottoman Empire such views were seen as challenges to the sultan’s spiritual and political authority. Suleiman I opposed those who disputed his religious authority as the Sufi perfect man, the redeemer and renewer of the age. Two of the three trials against Sufi dissenters during this period—that of Molla Kabiz and Ismail Masuki—occurred during the first twenty years of Suleiman I’s reign, when propaganda at court was anything but what we would today recognise as normative Sunni Islam.

paragraphs.source_en: AN ISLAMIC REFORMATION? In addition to the ubiquitous use of millenarian claims in both East and West, the sixteenth century was characterised by a challenge to the right to call oneself a true believer. Following the Reformation, Christianity in Western and Central Europe split into the Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist churches. As religious rivals pursuing common strategies and goals, each church promoted piety and individual spirituality, the internalisation of church teachings, the drawing of dichotomies between faiths, and the quest for uniform orthodoxy. They utilised violence to ensure religious homogeneity in the territories they ruled. Book burnings, inquisitions, heresy trials, the persecution of dissenters, and the 156 THE OTTOMANS burning of ‘witches’ were frequent and vicious.
